solution: Deadlock needs an even process i holding [latex]R_i[/latex] and waiting for [latex]R_{i+2}[/latex], while an odd process j holds [latex]R_{n-j}=R_{i+2}[/latex] and waits for [latex]R_{n-j-2}=R_i[/latex]. So j = n [latex]-[/latex] i [latex]-[/latex] 2 must be odd, with both i, j [latex]\lt[/latex] k. - n = 21, k = 12: i = 8, j = 11 works [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] deadlock possible. - n = 40 or 20: j = n [latex]-[/latex] i [latex]-[/latex] 2 is even [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] impossible. - n = 41, k = 19: i + j = 39 needs one of them [latex]\ge[/latex] 20 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] impossible. Answer: n = 21, k = 12 Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
solution_html:
Deadlock needs an even process i holding [latex]R_i[/latex] and waiting for [latex]R_{i+2}[/latex], while an odd process j holds [latex]R_{n-j}=R_{i+2}[/latex] and waits for [latex]R_{n-j-2}=R_i[/latex]. So j = n [latex]-[/latex] i [latex]-[/latex] 2 must be odd, with both i, j [latex]\lt[/latex] k.

- n = 21, k = 12: i = 8, j = 11 works [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] deadlock possible.
- n = 40 or 20: j = n [latex]-[/latex] i [latex]-[/latex] 2 is even [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] impossible.
- n = 41, k = 19: i + j = 39 needs one of them [latex]\ge[/latex] 20 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] impossible.

Answer: n = 21, k = 12

question: In a triangle [latex]PQR,PS[/latex] is the angle bisector of [latex]\angle QPR \text{ and } \angle QPS =60^\circ[/latex]. What is the length of [latex]PS[/latex] ?
solution: [latex]\angle QPR=120^\circ[/latex]. Area of PQR = area of PQS + area of PSR: [latex]\frac12 rq\sin120^\circ=\frac12 r\cdot PS\sin60^\circ+\frac12 q\cdot PS\sin60^\circ[/latex] Since [latex]\sin120^\circ=\sin60^\circ[/latex]: [latex]rq=PS(r+q)\Rightarrow PS=\frac{qr}{q+r}[/latex] Answer: [latex]\frac{qr}{q+r}[/latex] Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
solution_html:
[latex]\angle QPR=120^\circ[/latex]. Area of PQR = area of PQS + area of PSR:

[latex]\frac12 rq\sin120^\circ=\frac12 r\cdot PS\sin60^\circ+\frac12 q\cdot PS\sin60^\circ[/latex]

Since [latex]\sin120^\circ=\sin60^\circ[/latex]: [latex]rq=PS(r+q)\Rightarrow PS=\frac{qr}{q+r}[/latex]

Answer: [latex]\frac{qr}{q+r}[/latex]

question: Consider the following array. [latex]\begin{array}{|l|l|l|l|l|l|l|l|}  \hline 23&32&45&69&72&73&89&97 \\ \hline\end{array}[/latex] Which algorithm out of the following options uses the least number of comparisons (among the array elements) to sort the above array in ascending order?

options.label: D
options.text: Quicksort using the last element as pivot

solution: The array is already sorted. - Insertion sort : each element is compared once with its left neighbour [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] n [latex]-[/latex] 1 = 7 comparisons (best case). - Selection sort always does n(n [latex]-[/latex] 1)/2 = 28. - Merge sort needs more than 7 (about 12 here). - Quicksort with the last element as pivot on sorted input is the worst case (28). Answer: Insertion sort Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
solution_html:
The array is already sorted.
- Insertion sort: each element is compared once with its left neighbour [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] n [latex]-[/latex] 1 = 7 comparisons (best case).
- Selection sort always does n(n [latex]-[/latex] 1)/2 = 28.
- Merge sort needs more than 7 (about 12 here).
- Quicksort with the last element as pivot on sorted input is the worst case (28).

Answer: Insertion sort

question: The directional derivative of the field [latex]u(x,y,z)=x^{2}-3xy[/latex] in the direction of the vector [latex](\hat{i}+\hat{j}-2\hat{k})[/latex] and point (2, -1, 4) is _________.
solution: [latex]\begin{aligned}u (x, y, z)&=x^{2}-3yz \\  \triangledown u&=2x\hat{i}-3z\hat{j}-3y\hat{k} \\  \triangledown ul_{at\: \left ( 2,\, -1\, 4 \right )}&=4\hat{i}+12\hat{j}-3\hat{k}\\ &\text{Directional derivative}\\   &= \left ( 4\hat{i}+12\hat{j}-3\hat{k} \right ).\frac{\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}}{\sqrt{6}} \\   &= \frac{4-12-6}{\sqrt{6}} =-\frac{14}{\sqrt{6}} \\   &= -\frac{7\sqrt{6}}{3}=-5.715\end{aligned}[/latex]

question:
Given a function [latex]\varphi =\frac{1}{2}(x^2+y^2+z^2) [/latex] in threedimensional Cartesian space, the value of the
surface integral [latex]\oiint_{S}{\hat{n}.\triangledown \varphi dS}[/latex] where S is the surface of a sphere of unit radius and
[latex]\hat{n}[/latex] is the outward unit normal vector on S, is
solution:
[latex] \begin{aligned}
 \varphi &=\frac{1}{2}(x^2+y^2+z^2)\\
\triangledown \varphi &=(x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}+z\hat{k})=\bar{F}\\
\oiint_{S}(\triangledown \varphi\cdot \bar{n})dS&=\int \int _v\int Div\; \bar{F} dv\\
&=\int \int \int 3dv\\
&=3v\\
&=3\left ( \frac{4}{3} \pi \right )=4\pi
\end{aligned}[/latex]

question: The response of the system [latex]G(s)=\frac{s-2}{(s+1)(s+3)}[/latex] to the unit step input u(t) is y(t). The value of [latex]\frac{dy}{dt}[/latex] at t=[latex]0^{+}[/latex] is _________
solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} L\left(\frac{d y}{d t}\right) &=(s Y(s)-y(0)) \\ Y(s) &=G(s) \times \frac{1}{s}=\frac{s-2}{s(s+1)(s+3)} \\ y(0)&=\lim _{s \rightarrow \infty} s Y(s) \\ \text{(Applying } & \text{initial value theorem) } \\ &=\lim _{s \rightarrow \infty} \frac{s-2}{(s+1)(s+3)} \\ &=\frac{\left(1-\frac{2}{s}\right)}{s\left(1+\frac{1}{s}\right)\left(1+\frac{3}{s}\right)} \\ y(0)&=0 \\ L\left(\frac{d y}{d t}\right) &=s Y(s)=\frac{s \times(s-2)}{s(s+1)(s+3)} \\ &=\frac{s-2}{(s+1)(s+3)} \\ \left.\frac{d y}{d t}\right|_{t=0} &=\lim _{s \rightarrow \infty} s L\left(\frac{d y}{d t}\right) \\ &=\lim _{s \rightarrow \infty} \frac{s \times(s-2)}{(s+1)(s+3)}\\ &=\frac{\left(1-\frac{2}{s}\right)}{\left(1+\frac{1}{s}\right)\left(1+\frac{3}{s}\right)}=1 \end{aligned}[/latex]
solution_html: [latex]\begin{aligned} L\left(\frac{d y}{d t}\right) &=(s Y(s)-y(0)) \\ Y(s) &=G(s) \times \frac{1}{s}=\frac{s-2}{s(s+1)(s+3)} \\ y(0)&=\lim _{s \rightarrow \infty} s Y(s) \\ \text{(Applying } & \text{initial value theorem) } \\ &=\lim _{s \rightarrow \infty} \frac{s-2}{(s+1)(s+3)} \\ &=\frac{\left(1-\frac{2}{s}\right)}{s\left(1+\frac{1}{s}\right)\left(1+\frac{3}{s}\right)} \\ y(0)&=0 \\ L\left(\frac{d y}{d t}\right) &=s Y(s)=\frac{s \times(s-2)}{s(s+1)(s+3)} \\ &=\frac{s-2}{(s+1)(s+3)} \\ \left.\frac{d y}{d t}\right|_{t=0} &=\lim _{s \rightarrow \infty} s L\left(\frac{d y}{d t}\right) \\ &=\lim _{s \rightarrow \infty} \frac{s \times(s-2)}{(s+1)(s+3)}\\ &=\frac{\left(1-\frac{2}{s}\right)}{\left(1+\frac{1}{s}\right)\left(1+\frac{3}{s}\right)}=1 \end{aligned}[/latex]

question: Consider two function [latex]f(n)=n^{1+\frac{1}{\log n}}[/latex] [latex]g(n)=n \log ( \log n)[/latex] Which of the following is/are true? [MSQ Question]
solution:
In this types of complex function, we can not directly compare given functions [latex]f(n)[/latex]
 and [latex]g(n)[/latex] by putting value of n. So, we have to use the concept of taking log on both function  [latex]f(n)[/latex]
 and [latex]g(n)[/latex] and then compare both to find the relation in terms of which function is of higher order. [latex]\begin{aligned} \log (f(n))&=\log (n^{1+\frac{1}{\log n}}) \\ &= \left ( 1+\frac{1}{\log n} \right ) \log n\\ &= \log n+1 \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} \log (g(n))&=\log ( n \log (\log n)) \\ &= \log n + \log ( \log (\log n)) \end{aligned}[/latex] Now, comparing both function is easy by just taking differen value of n. NOTE: Take higher value of n when comparing both function and choose value of n which makes calculation easy. For example [latex]n=2^{2^{2^{100}}}[/latex] (Value of n is selected such that  calculation of three times log become easy) Then, value of [latex]\begin{aligned}\log (f(n))&=\log(2^{2^{2^{100}}})+1\\& =2^{2^{100}}+1\end{aligned}[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned}\log (g(n))&=\log (2^{2^{2^{100}}}) + \log ( \log (\log (2^{2^{2^{100}}}))) \\ &=2^{2^{100}}+ \log (\log {2^{2^{100}}})\\ & =2^{2^{100}}+\log( {2^{100}})\\ &=2^{2^{100}}+100\end{aligned}[/latex]. Based on above anlysis, we can say that, [latex]g(n)[/latex] is of higher order compared to [latex]f(n)[/latex]. Option A: [latex]f(n)=O(g(n))[/latex] is true as said above [latex]g(n)[/latex] is of higher order than  [latex]f(n)[/latex] Option B: [latex]g(n)=O(f(n))[/latex] is false. Option C: [latex]f(n)=\Theta (g(n))[/latex] is false as [latex]f(n)=\Omega (g(n))[/latex] is not true. Option D: [latex]g(n)=\Omega (f(n))[/latex] is true as said above [latex]g(n)[/latex] is higher order than  [latex]f(n)[/latex].
